verses.translation_literal: Of David, a psalm. Loyalty and justice I will sing; to you, YHWH, I will make music.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm of David. Two words, and I will build my song on them: faithful love, and justice. To you, LORD, I lift my voice, and to you the strings will answer.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open this one as a king's oath, not a hymn of private feeling. The first two words, chesed and mishpat, are the two pillars of ancient Near Eastern kingship: loyalty to the covenant and the verdict that gives each person what is theirs. Kings across Mesopotamia and Egypt boasted of both in royal inscriptions, so the audience hears a coronation vow before they hear a song. The pairing is also deliberately ambiguous, and the tradition knew it: Rashi hears the singer praising God for kindness and equally for judgment ('blessed is the true Judge'), while Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri hear the king describing his own rule. Play both; the psalm will go on to describe the second.

The KJV 'mercy and judgment' softens both words. Chesed is not pity but loyal, bound-in-covenant love, and mishpat is justice as an act, not a verdict suffered; 'judgment' sounds like a punishment, which is how English readers misread it. The KJV also hides the double verb: the first 'sing' (shir) is the voice, the second (zamar) is music with an instrument, the root behind mizmor, the 'psalm' of the title. The Hebrew counts this superscription as verse 1, which is why the KJV starts at 101:0.

philological_notes.note: Loyalty that keeps a covenant, kindness owed within a bond, not generic mercy. Here it pairs with mishpat as the two things the singer will celebrate, whether in God or in himself as king.
To make music, to sing with accompaniment. It repeats the idea of 'sing' (shir) in a stronger, instrumental key and shares its root with mizmor, the psalm of the title.

verses.translation_literal: I will give heed in a way of the blameless: when will you come to me? I will walk about in the integrity of my heart in the midst of my house.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will study the road of the blameless, and I will wait, and I will ask: when will you come to me? Until you do, I will walk my own rooms with a whole heart, the heart I carry through my own house.
verses.directors_commentary:
The king begins with himself. Ashkilah is more than 'behave wisely': it means to pay close attention until understanding arrives, to study the blameless way as a student studies a craft. Then the line breaks. 'When will you come to me?' is the psalm's hinge, and it is only three words in Hebrew, without an object. The tradition split on who is coming: God, with the spirit that makes a ruler fit to rule (Radak), or the blameless way itself, becoming so habitual that it comes to the walker (Ibn Ezra, Malbim). Direct the actor to let the question hang; it is a real longing, not a rhetorical flourish.

The KJV smooths this into an exclamation, 'O when wilt thou come unto me?', and then calls the word tamim, 'perfect'. It means whole, unblemished, the word used for sacrificial animals without defect, so the 'perfect way' is the undivided way. The last phrase is the test case: 'in the midst of my house'. A palace was where a king could be seen, and also where he could not be seen. Rashi's reading is that the heart is as whole in secret as in public. Walking back and forth inside the house is a private act, which makes it the real examination.

philological_notes.note: To give heed, to look attentively and so understand. Radak glosses it 'I will give my heart to understanding'. The cohortative form is a resolve.
Whole, complete, without defect. It is the word for an unblemished sacrificial animal and for a person whose conduct has no break between what is shown and what is meant.
'When will you come to me?' A bare question with no stated object; the commentators divide between God's coming (the spirit of rule) and the way's coming as second nature.

verses.translation_literal: I will not set before my eyes a thing of worthlessness; the doing of swervings I hate; it will not cling to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will not set before my eyes anything worthless. I hate the doing of crooked things, the quiet turning-aside. It will not cling to me.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the inner house to the eyes. Seeing in Hebrew is choosing: what a king sets 'before his eyes' is the standard by which he decides, the way an ancient ruler set a model, a statute, or a goal in front of himself. Radak even reads it physically, as the faculty of imagination. So the vow is not 'I will not look at evil' but 'I will not make worthlessness my aim'.

The key word is beliyya'al. The KJV 'wicked thing' is a loose paraphrase; the Hebrew is 'a word/thing of beliyya'al', literally worthlessness, nothing-good, and later tradition made it a name for Belial, a demonic figure. Here it still means plain worthlessness, the opposite of what a king's eyes should rest on. 'Them that turn aside' in the KJV turns sitim from deeds into people; the Hebrew says 'the doing of swervings', the act of veering off the road, from the same root as the sota of Numbers 5:12, the wife who 'turns aside' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak). The final verb is physical and unpleasant: dabaq is to stick like glue, to cling like a leech. The king hates the doing of it and refuses to let it stick.

philological_notes.note: Worthlessness, 'without profit'. Not yet a personal name here. It names the kind of aim the king will not put in front of himself; the KJV 'wicked' misses the idea of emptiness.
Swervings, deviations. The traditional commentators link it to satah 'to turn aside' (Num 5:12) and to Proverbs 7:25 'turn not aside to her ways'; the doer is one who leaves the straight road.
To stick, cling, cleave, as flesh to bone or a man to his wife. The refusal is that evil should adhere to him.

verses.translation_literal: A twisted heart will depart from me; evil I will not know.
verses.translation_dramatic: A twisted heart will turn away from me. Evil I will not know. I will not even learn its name.
verses.directors_commentary:
Short, flat, and final: the vow narrows from conduct to company. Two readings sit together. One: the king's own twisted heart, the crooked impulse, will leave him (Malbim). The other, more common among the medieval commentators: a person with a twisted heart will leave his presence, because the king will not keep him among his acquaintances (Radak, Metzudat David). 'Know' (yada) is the verb of covenant familiarity: to know someone is to be their friend and associate, which is why a 'friend' in Hebrew can be a 'known one' (mode'a, Metzudat David). So 'I will not know evil' means 'I will not befriend, I will not promote'.

The KJV 'froward' is archaic (it means 'turned away'), and 'I will not know a wicked person' supplies 'person' where the Hebrew has a bare, abstract 'evil', ra'. The ASV got closer: 'no evil thing'. The Hebrew 'twisted' (iqqesh) is the crooked as opposed to the straight, the opposite of the yashar road the king has been praising. Say it without heat; the quiet is the menace.

philological_notes.note: Twisted, crooked, perverse. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'bent'. It is the moral opposite of the straight (yashar) way.
To know in the sense of familiar association: to acknowledge, befriend, employ. The commentators take 'I will not know evil' as 'I will not have an evil person among my acquaintances'.

verses.translation_literal: One who slanders in secret his neighbor, [obj] him I will destroy; high of eyes and wide of heart, [obj] him I am not able [to endure].
verses.translation_dramatic: The one who whispers against his neighbor in the dark, behind a hand, behind a closed door: him I will end. And the one whose eyes sit high and whose heart has grown wide with itself: him I cannot bear.
verses.directors_commentary:
The king speaks in two halves, and both begin with the object held at the front: "him," pointing at the man, and then the verb. Play it as a finger raised twice. The first target is the slanderer "in secret": in a palace, where access to the king and gossip about rivals were the main currency, a whispered accusation could ruin a man without ever being tested in court. Radak imagines exactly this: a man who informs against his fellow privately, to convict him under the laws of the kingship, and he adds that this king would not punish anyone without witnesses, since even a true word from a single informant is a sin (Radak on Psalm 101:5). Malbim reads the verse the same way: unlike most rulers, this one does not accept slander, but removes the slanderer.

The KJV "cut off" is accurate here. The verb "atzmit" means to put an end to, to destroy, and Metzudat Zion, Metzudat David and Meiri all gloss it with the verb karat, "cut off" (Metzudat Zion cites "he will destroy them in their evil" from Psalm 94); the ASV's "destroy" and the BBE's "put to death" are the stronger end of the same range. The same verb returns in verse 8, where the king silences all the wicked of the land every morning: the slanderer is the first example of that program. The second half is not about speech but posture. "High of eyes" is a lifted gaze, looking down on others; "wide of heart" is a heart with room for everything it desires. The KJV's "high look" and "proud heart" capture the first well enough but flatten the second: the Hebrew image is spatial, a heart stretched wide, which Radak and Meiri take as appetite for the pleasures of the world. Note the change of verb: the slanderer is destroyed, but the proud man is merely one the king "is not able" to bear. The final "lo ukhal" is open: Rashi hears "I cannot have him as my companion," Radak "I cannot bear to see him."

philological_notes.note: A verb of ending or destroying; here the king's act against the slanderer. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'cutting off', with a parallel in Psalm 94, and the verb recurs in verse 8. It is a firm act, not an emotional dislike, and contrasts with the weaker 'I am not able' used for the proud.

Two bodily images for arrogance: eyes lifted high and a heart made wide. Radak reads the eyes as looking after the desires of the world and the wide heart as giving them room within; Metzudat David takes the first as pride and the second as one who covets everything. Meiri quotes a saying that the eye and the heart are the two panders of sin.

'I am able', with the complement left out; the verse says 'him I am not able' and lets the hearer supply 'to endure'. The commentators supply 'to see him' or 'to bear him' (Radak, Ibn Ezra), 'to bear' (Metzudat David) or 'to have him as my companion' (Rashi).

token_glosses.gloss: I will put an end to

verses.translation_literal: My eyes [are] on the faithful of the land, to dwell with me; one who walks in a way [that is] blameless, he will serve me.
verses.translation_dramatic: But my eyes go out to the faithful of the land, and they search for them. Let them come and sit beside me, under my roof. And the one who walks a blameless road: he, and no other, will serve me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns from the hand raised against to the eye turned toward. Verse 5 was about whom the king removes; this is about whom he looks for. Radak reads the sentence as an active search: the wicked he keeps away from his house and his seat, but the faithful he sends for, from wherever they are, to bring them to him. The KJV "shall be upon" is a fair rendering, but it adds a verb; the Hebrew has none, just "my eyes on the faithful of the land."

"Faithful of the land" is also broader than "faithful" alone, and Malbim makes the political point: rulers of the ancient East chose counselors loyal to the ruler to gather wealth, while this king chooses those loyal to the land and its people, and will bring them to sit with him as advisers. Meiri likewise sees "dwell with me" as membership of the king's council and secrets. The second half sets the standard for service. The KJV's "perfect way" is archaic; "tamim" is blameless, whole, without defect, the word used of sacrificial animals, and here of a road with no fault in it. In a court, those who served at the table, at the door and at the judgment seat stood closest to the king, so the king's household is only as clean as the people he admits to it. Ibn Ezra says it of the throne of justice: when the king sits in judgment, none but the one who walks the blameless way will serve him and stand before him. The ASV's "minister unto me" is closer to the verb's formal service than the KJV's plain "serve."

philological_notes.note: 'The faithful of the land': a participle of a verb of firmness and trust. Malbim reads it as 'faithful to the land and its people', in contrast to counselors faithful only to a ruler; Meiri takes it as the righteous and pious who join the king's counsel.
Whole, complete, blameless. The KJV 'perfect' now suggests flawlessness; the sense is integrity without a flaw, applied here to a person's whole way of life.

'He will serve me': the verb of attending on a superior. Ibn Ezra reads it in the setting of the throne of judgment: when the king sits in judgment, only the one who walks the blameless way will serve him and stand before him at the time of judgment. Radak adds that the king will take for his service only the good.

verses.translation_literal: He will not dwell in the midst of my house, one who does deceit; one who speaks lies will not be established before my eyes.
verses.translation_dramatic: No one who works deceit will live in my house. No one who speaks lies will stand firm before my eyes.
verses.directors_commentary:
The household mirrors the court. The verbs of the last verse, 'dwell' and 'serve', return in the negative: the faithful will dwell with the king, the deceitful will not dwell in his house. 'In the midst of my house' also echoes verse 2, the place where the king walks in integrity, so the king's own interior and the people he admits to it must match. Note the two kinds of liar: the one who does deceit (an action, a trick) and the one who speaks lies (words), as a Hebrew poet would balance deed and speech.

The final verb is a gem that the KJV 'tarry in my sight' ruins. Yikkon, from the root kun, means to be set firm, established, made stable, the verb used for a throne being established. The liar will not be established before the king's eyes: nothing he builds there will stand. The KJV turns a promise of instability into a mere waiting room. Radak puts the force bluntly: he will not even see him, still less have him as a resident.

philological_notes.note: Deceit, treachery, a slackness of dealing that betrays trust. Meiri takes it as the noun 'deceit' (or the doer of deceit, if a participle).
To be set firm, established, secure, the verb of a throne or a house standing. The KJV 'tarry' loses the idea of stability.

verses.translation_literal: To the mornings I will destroy all the wicked of the land, to cut off from the city of YHWH all the doers of iniquity.
verses.translation_dramatic: Morning after morning I will silence the wicked of the land, until every worker of iniquity has been cut off from the city of the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The vow ends at the city gate, at dawn. In Israel and its neighbours, the king's morning was when justice was done: Jeremiah 21:12 says 'execute justice in the morning', and Ibn Ezra reads 'lebbaqarim' as the daily court sitting. 'To the mornings' is a plural, a repeated daily act: not one great purge but a steady discipline, as Rashi says, 'little by little'. The KJV 'early destroy' reads it as haste, and the ASV 'morning by morning' is correct; Metzudat David hears energy in it.

The verb is the same atzmit from verse 5, so the psalm bookends its list of those the king will not tolerate. It is followed by 'cut off' (karat), the covenant vocabulary: those who are cut off are removed from the people, as a covenant is 'cut'. 'City of the LORD' is Jerusalem (Radak, Meiri, Targum), the place where YHWH's name dwells, and the stakes are purity of the place. The KJV's 'wicked doers' misrenders 'workers of iniquity', poale aven: aven is trouble, wrongdoing that harms others. Read it as a closing refrain, the final punishment of the very ones named in verses 3 to 7. Remember it is a king speaking his own intent, an aspiration for a court he hopes to run, rather than a report of what he has done.

philological_notes.note: 'To the mornings': every morning, repeatedly. It names the daily hour of judgment (see Jer 21:12), not a single dawn.
'City of YHWH', taken by the commentators and the Targum as Jerusalem. The text does not name the city.
Workers of iniquity: those whose business is harm and trouble; a stock phrase of the Psalms for the wicked as a class.
